name: Deposit insurance and banking stabilization
stated_intent: Restore confidence in banks and protect small depositors after widespread bank suspensions.
mechanism: Banking Act of 1933 created the FDIC; federal deposit insurance began January 1, 1934 with $2,500 initial coverage.
recorded_outcome: The FDIC records approximately 9,000 bank suspensions during 1930–1933 and nine insured-bank failures in 1934. Depositor confidence improved following a package of actions.
benefit: Protection against loss of insured deposits and reduced incentive for insured depositors to run.
tradeoff_or_risk: Deposit insurance creates moral-hazard concerns without complementary supervision and risk-based premiums.
caveat: Before/after numbers span different regimes and definitions. Bank holiday, recapitalization and other changes occurred contemporaneously; do not assign full causal effect to insurance alone.
source_names: FDIC 90-year historical timeline | FDIC A Brief History of Deposit Insurance

name: Monetary Control Act and deposit-rate deregulation
stated_intent: Remove deposit-rate ceilings that penalized savers, help banks compete for deposits and strengthen monetary control.
mechanism: Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act of 1980 phased out interest-rate caps and extended reserve requirements and discount-window access.
recorded_outcome: Banks gained flexibility to attract deposits; the law also expanded some thrift powers and coincided with heightened pressure on the thrift model.
benefit: Greater access to market-rate deposit products and broader coverage of Fed monetary tools.
tradeoff_or_risk: Higher funding costs and expanded permissions increased stress and risk for some institutions already exposed to long-term, fixed-rate mortgages.
caveat: Interest-rate shocks predated the act; do not treat the legislation as the sole cause of subsequent failures.
source_names: Federal Reserve History: Monetary Control Act | Federal Reserve History: Regulation Q

name: Garn–St Germain Depository Institutions Act
stated_intent: Help troubled banks and thrifts adapt to high interest rates, competition and losses on legacy mortgage portfolios.
mechanism: Authorized new deposit accounts and expanded eligible thrift assets and activities, along with emergency assistance tools.
recorded_outcome: The changes improved flexibility and competition but some provisions amplified risk-taking and supervisory difficulties; the broader savings-and-loan crisis continued.
benefit: More attractive deposit accounts and additional restructuring options for institutions facing stress.
tradeoff_or_risk: Additional powers given to fragile institutions could increase potential losses when combined with weak supervision and forbearance.
caveat: S&L losses reflected interest-rate shocks, asset/liability mismatch, fraud, and regulatory failures, not one law alone.
source_names: Federal Reserve History: Garn–St Germain Act | Federal Reserve History: Savings and Loan Crisis

name: FIRREA and FDICIA response
stated_intent: Resolve failed thrifts, restore confidence in deposit insurance, and force earlier supervisory intervention to limit public losses.
mechanism: FIRREA reorganized thrift supervision and resolution; FDICIA added prompt corrective action and least-cost resolution requirements.
recorded_outcome: The reforms changed supervisory processes and resolution powers after a crisis that imposed large taxpayer costs.
benefit: Clearer failure-resolution responsibilities and capital-triggered intervention framework.
tradeoff_or_risk: Early intervention and least-cost constraints can present implementation challenges during system-wide shocks.
caveat: A statutory reform is not itself proof that later systemic crises were prevented; assess outcomes with time-series and independent studies.
review_status: legal changes verified; impacts need deeper measurement
source_names: Federal Reserve History: FDICIA | FDIC: 1980–1989 chronology
